topics.title: Cells and the microscope
topics.notes:
A compound light microscope has an eyepiece (ocular), objective lenses, a stage with clips, a condenser, a light source, and coarse and fine focusing knobs. Total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective power. The specimen sits closest to the objective lens, and high-power objectives have short focal lengths. An electron gun belongs to an electron microscope, not a light microscope. Fluorescence microscopy uses a stained specimen that absorbs light and re-emits it at a longer wavelength. For unit conversions, 1 mm = 1,000 µm, so 0.5 mm = 500 µm.

Organelles and their jobs: the cell membrane controls what enters and leaves; the nucleus holds the DNA and controls the cell; mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration; ribosomes make proteins; rough ER carries ribosomes while smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies; the Golgi body packages materials; lysosomes hold digestive enzymes; peroxisomes break down fatty acids and make hydrogen peroxide; vacuoles store water, food and wastes.

Plant cells differ from animal cells in having a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a large central vacuole. Higher plants lack centrioles. Fungal walls are made of chitin and bacterial walls of peptidoglycan.

Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) have no nucleus. Their DNA lies in a region called the nucleoid, and they have no membrane-bound organelles. Every cell, prokaryote or eukaryote, has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes. Animals, plants and fungi are all eukaryotes, so they share a defined nucleus.

The two focusing knobs are the coarse and fine adjustment knobs. With a ×10 ocular and a ×20 objective the total magnification is ×200. Specimens are prepared by fixing, embedding, sectioning and staining.

KEY FORMULA: Magnification = eyepiece × objective;  1 mm = 1,000 µm;  prokaryotes: nucleoid, no nucleus
topics.keyFormula: Magnification = eyepiece × objective;  1 mm = 1,000 µm;  prokaryotes: nucleoid, no nucleus

topics.title: Bacteria, cyanobacteria and viruses
topics.notes:
Bacteria were first seen by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. Most have a cell wall of peptidoglycan (murein). The Gram stain separates them: Gram-positive cells have a thick peptidoglycan wall and stay purple, while Gram-negative cells have a thin wall and an outer membrane and stain pink. Many bacteria also carry plasmids, small circular DNA molecules separate from the main chromosome. Actinomycetes are filamentous bacteria that were once mistaken for fungi because of their branching mycelium.

Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic eubacteria. Gloeocapsa is unicellular or colonial, while Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria are filamentous. Heterocysts contain nitrogenase and fix nitrogen, and akinetes are thick-walled resting cells that store food. Archaebacteria include halophiles, methanogens and thermoacidophiles such as Sulfolobus, but not cyanobacteria. Rickettsias and chlamydias are tiny prokaryotes placed in Kingdom Monera. The three domains of life are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.

Viruses are not cells. Each has a protein coat (capsid) around a core of either DNA or RNA, never both, and some also have an envelope, spikes or tail fibres. Outside a host cell the particle is called a virion. Viruses lack ribosomes and can replicate only inside living host cells. Retroviruses use the enzyme reverse transcriptase to make DNA from their RNA.

Penicillin kills growing bacteria by blocking the building of the peptidoglycan wall. Cyanobacteria were the first organisms to carry out oxygenic photosynthesis. Actinomycetes are bacteria, not fungi. Chloroxybacteria are eubacteria, not archaebacteria. Bacteria divide by binary fission and have no alternation of generations, and viruses cannot divide at all.

KEY FORMULA: Virus = capsid (protein) + DNA or RNA;  Gram+ = thick peptidoglycan = purple
topics.keyFormula: Virus = capsid (protein) + DNA or RNA;  Gram+ = thick peptidoglycan = purple

topics.title: Fungi and lichens
topics.notes:
Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs that feed by absorption: they secrete enzymes onto their food (extracellular digestion) and absorb the products. Their cell walls are made of chitin and their food reserve is glycogen. The body is made of hyphae, which together form a mycelium. Hyphae with cross-walls are septate, and hyphae without them are coenocytic. Parasitic fungi absorb from their host through haustoria. Yeasts are unicellular. Fungi are the main decomposers on land.

The main divisions are: Zygomycota (Mucor and Rhizopus, the black bread mould), Ascomycota (sac fungi, including yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae), Basidiomycota (club fungi: mushrooms and puffballs) and Deuteromycota (fungi with no known sexual stage). Pyrophilous fungi grow on burnt ground.

In the sexual cycle, plasmogamy (cytoplasm fuses) gives a heterokaryotic phase, then karyogamy (nuclei fuse) gives a diploid zygote, which undergoes meiosis to give haploid spores. A lichen is a partnership between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium. Lichens are very sensitive to SO₂, so they are used as indicators of air pollution. A mycorrhiza is a symbiosis between a fungus and the roots of a higher plant.

Deuteromycota are the "imperfect fungi" because no sexual stage is known. Ascomycota make their asci inside a fruiting body called an ascocarp, which can be cup-shaped and open (apothecium), flask-shaped with an opening called an ostiole (perithecium) or completely closed and spherical (cleistothecium). Fungi have no chlorophyll and no true roots, stems or leaves.

KEY FORMULA: Fungi: chitin wall, glycogen store;  plasmogamy → karyogamy → meiosis
topics.keyFormula: Fungi: chitin wall, glycogen store;  plasmogamy → karyogamy → meiosis

topics.title: Algae
topics.notes:
Algae are placed in divisions mainly by their pigments, their storage product, their flagella (number and position) and their cell wall. Chlorophyta (green algae) have chlorophylls a and b and store starch. Phaeophyta (brown algae) store laminarin. Rhodophyta (red algae) store floridean starch and yield agar and carrageenan, which are used in culture media and food. Euglenophyta (Euglena) have chlorophylls a and b, store paramylon and have a flexible pellicle instead of a cell wall.

Chlamydomonas and Volvox are both motile green algae (Chlorophyta). Each cell of Oedogonium has one net-like chloroplast with several pyrenoids. The way an alga reproduces is not one of the criteria for placing it in a division.

Alginates come from the cell walls of brown algae. Carrageenan comes from red algae, not green. Green algae and land plants share chlorophylls a and b, carotenoids and starch storage, which is the evidence that land plants arose from green algae.

KEY FORMULA: Storage: green = starch, brown = laminarin, red = floridean starch, Euglena = paramylon
topics.keyFormula: Storage: green = starch, brown = laminarin, red = floridean starch, Euglena = paramylon

topics.title: Bryophytes and pteridophytes
topics.notes:
Bryophytes (liverworts, hornworts and mosses) are simple land plants without xylem or phloem. The gametophyte is the dominant, leafy or thalloid phase. The sporophyte grows on the gametophyte and depends on it for food. Sperm swim in a film of water to reach the egg, so they need dew or rain. Monoecious mosses bear antheridia and archegonia on the same plant. The moss capsule has a central columella. A moss spore grows into a thread-like protonema. In Marchantia, gemmae cups on the thallus produce gemmae for vegetative reproduction. Bryophytes and green algae have the same photosynthetic pigments.

Pteridophytes (ferns and allies) are the first vascular plants. The diploid sporophyte is dominant, with xylem and phloem (phloem has sieve cells but no companion cells) and lignified walls. They reproduce by spores, make no seeds, and have a small free-living gametophyte called a prothallus, so both generations are independent. The fern rhizome is a stem.

Divisions of pteridophytes: Psilotophyta (whisk ferns), Lycopodiophyta (club mosses), Equisetophyta (horsetails, or scouring rushes) and Filicophyta (ferns). Coniferophyta is a gymnosperm division, not a pteridophyte one. The protostele is the most primitive stele. Heterospory is the production of large megaspores and small microspores. Some extinct "seed ferns" bore seeds.

Liverworts and other bryophytes have no stele. Leptoids and hydroids (simple conducting cells) occur only in some mosses. A leaf that bears sporangia is a sporophyll.

KEY FORMULA: Bryophytes: gametophyte dominant, no vascular tissue;  pteridophytes: sporophyte dominant, vascular, spores
topics.keyFormula: Bryophytes: gametophyte dominant, no vascular tissue;  pteridophytes: sporophyte dominant, vascular, spores

topics.title: Gymnosperms and angiosperms
topics.notes:
Gymnosperms have "naked" seeds and are all woody; their wood is softwood. There are four divisions: Cycadophyta, Ginkgophyta, Coniferophyta and Gnetophyta. Conifers (pines and junipers) are the largest and most economically important group, and they are found mainly in temperate and cold regions. The female cone (megastrobilus) has a central axis with ovuliferous scales that carry the ovules.

Gnetophyta contain three very different genera: Gnetum, Ephedra and Welwitschia. They have vessel elements, ovules with two integuments and a kind of double fertilization, so they are thought closest to the angiosperms. Welwitschia keeps its two original leaves for its whole life. Palm-like leaves belong to the cycads.

In angiosperms the stamen is the microsporophyll and the carpel is the megasporophyll. Ovules develop inside the carpel. Double fertilization is the hallmark of the group, and hardwood comes from angiosperm trees. Bryophyllum can be propagated from its leaves. A maize seedling grown in the dark turns yellow (etiolated) because it cannot photosynthesize, and it dies once its food reserve runs out.

Monocot stems have scattered vascular bundles and no cambium, so they do not show secondary growth.

KEY FORMULA: Gymnosperms: naked seeds, softwood;  angiosperms: flowers, double fertilization, hardwood
topics.keyFormula: Gymnosperms: naked seeds, softwood;  angiosperms: flowers, double fertilization, hardwood

topics.title: Plant life cycles
topics.notes:
The three life-cycle types differ in where meiosis happens. In a haplontic cycle, meiosis occurs in the zygote (zygotic meiosis), so the body is haploid and only the zygote is diploid. This is the most primitive type and is found in Volvox, Spirogyra, Ulothrix and Chlamydomonas.

In a diplontic cycle, meiosis produces the gametes (gametic meiosis) and the body is diploid. It is seen in some algae such as Fucus and, in this course, in seed plants.

In a haplodiplontic cycle, meiosis produces spores (sporic meiosis) and there are two different bodies: a haploid gametophyte and a diploid sporophyte. This is called alternation of generations and is found in bryophytes and pteridophytes.

Only the haploid body is conspicuous in a haplontic cycle, and the zygote is the only diploid cell. The sporophyte (2n) makes spores by meiosis and the gametophyte (n) makes eggs and sperm by mitosis. Gametes are haploid, the normal somatic number is diploid, and the zygote grows into the sporophyte.

KEY FORMULA: Zygotic meiosis = haplontic;  gametic meiosis = diplontic;  sporic meiosis = haplodiplontic
topics.keyFormula: Zygotic meiosis = haplontic;  gametic meiosis = diplontic;  sporic meiosis = haplodiplontic

topics.title: Nutrition, symbiosis and biotic interactions
topics.notes:
Autotrophs make their own food: photoautotrophs use light, and chemoautotrophs use energy from chemical reactions. Heterotrophs feed on organic matter made by others: holozoic (ingesting food), saprophytic or saprotrophic (dead and decaying matter) and parasitic (living hosts). Saprophytes digest food outside the body and absorb the products. Mutualism is a relationship between organisms, not a mode of nutrition.

Interactions between species: mutualism (both benefit, for example clownfish and sea anemone, or coral and zooxanthellae), commensalism (one benefits and the other is unaffected), parasitism (one benefits and the other is harmed) and predation (the predator kills and eats its prey). Types of commensalism include phoresy (hitching a ride), metabiosis (using the remains of another organism, such as a hermit crab in an empty shell) and inquilinism (living in another's shelter).

Parasites living inside the host are endoparasites (tapeworms, and Plasmodium inside cells), and those on the outside are ectoparasites. Parasites cause an immune response in the host and occur in all habitats. Cuscuta is a parasitic plant. Competition can be intraspecific (same species) or interspecific (different species), and exploitative (using up a shared resource) or interference (directly blocking a rival). Closely linked partners adapt to each other through co-evolution.

Organisms get energy as light or as chemical energy. Animals feed holozoically (ingesting and digesting food internally).

KEY FORMULA: Mutualism +/+;  commensalism +/0;  parasitism +/−;  predation kills and eats
topics.keyFormula: Mutualism +/+;  commensalism +/0;  parasitism +/−;  predation kills and eats

topics.title: Classification and naming of organisms
topics.notes:
Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature: a genus name followed by a species epithet, such as Aspergillus niger. The ranks run Domain, Kingdom, Phylum (Division in plants), Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species, and species is the lowest major rank. Plant family names end in -aceae, for example Convolvulaceae (sweet potato) and Musaceae (plantain). Life is divided into three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.

Classification systems: the artificial system (Linnaeus) uses a few convenient characters; the natural system groups plants by overall similarity in form and reproductive characters; and the phylogenetic system reflects evolutionary relationships. Modern classification uses morphology, genetics and phylogenetics, but not the old doctrine of signatures. Classification gives each organism a unique name, aids memory and shows relationships.

In the five-kingdom system (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia), bacteria and cyanobacteria are in Monera and algae are placed in Protista in this course. Cryptogams are non-flowering plants and phanerogams are seed plants. Growth habits include herb, shrub, tree and climber. Zea mays is a plant, Saccharomyces is a fungus and Plasmodium and Amoeba are protists. Bread wheat is Triticum aestivum.

Linnaeus made the first widely accepted plant classification system and used the binomial system consistently. Protista is a mixed (polyphyletic) group and not all protists are algae. Herbaceous biennials are soft-stemmed plants that take two growing seasons to complete their life cycle.

KEY FORMULA: Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
topics.keyFormula: Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
